The high air under the roof is thick with steam, soft and white, blurring the ribs at the top of the frame.
Condensation sheets every pane overhead and runs down them in slow clear lines.
Fat drops fall from the ribs and land on the broad leaves below, each leaf holding a bright bead where one struck.
A warm wet haze hangs at chest height and softens everything at the far end of the house.
Steam creeps up between the floor slats and lies in a low white drift across the grating.
The wet air has gone the nearest glass soft grey with mist, clear only in one wiped arc.
Fine mist drifts out from the rail above the ferns and hangs there, catching the light before it falls.
Water sheets down the inside of the flank glass and runs into a brimming channel at its foot.
The floor grating is dark and soaked and steaming faintly along its whole length.
A pipe joint puffs steam in a small bright plume that thins out and joins the haze above.
The air is so heavy with wet that the light itself is visible in it, thick and soft between the leaves.
Every cold surface is beaded: the ribs, the chains, the brass rails, all of them holding rows of small clear drops.
Warmth rises off the beds in visible slow curls and wanders up toward the open vents.
A drop falls into the pool every few seconds and rings the surface in widening circles.
Steam has wrapped the upper catwalk so its far end is only a suggestion of plank and rail.
The glass immediately above the hottest bed is running freely, its water gathering into fat trembling drops along the rib.
Moisture has silvered the brass rail along the central bed, the metal gone dull and soft-looking where the air has settled on it.
The vent at the ridge stands open a crack and draws a thin tongue of steam up through it and out.
Beads on the underside of the catwalk planks have grown heavy enough to fall, dotting the leaves beneath in a slow irregular pattern.
The warmth inside has fogged the outer face of the glass so the garden beyond is only a green blur through it.
A long thread of water runs the length of one rib, pausing at each rivet before continuing down toward the gutter.
Where two panes meet at the ridge their condensation pools and falls as a thin curtain into the bed directly below.
The brass fittings at the base of the heating pipe are crusted with white mineral trace left by steam cooling there over many seasons.
Humid air has softened the edge of every shadow so the shadows themselves look wet, blurred at their margins across the stone floor.
The chain hanging from the vent wheel is dark with moisture and drips from its lowest link onto the gravel path.
Along the foot of the north glass the channel is full and still and reflects the panes above it in a shivering stripe.
The furthest bed is entirely lost in a low white cloud that sits at leaf level and moves only slowly.
Steam rising off the heated pipes has left a faint tide line of mineral grey on the glass just above them.
The cooler air near the door has caused a heavier condensation there, the panes running fast and the sill dark with it.
Each rivet along the arching rib holds its own small bead, the whole arc of them catching whatever light comes through the fogged glass.
A slow bloom of mist expands outward from the junction of the main supply pipe and the lateral, spreading and thinning as it rises.
The gravel between the beds is dark and glistening, individual stones bright where drops have struck them and gathered in the hollows.
Warm condensation on the brass overhead catch-plate has thickened into a slow amber bead running toward its lower edge.
The air near the heating pipes is hotter and thicker and visible as a shimmer that bends the far glass slightly out of true.
Mist has settled into the lower fern fronds and lies there in small still pools cupped by the curved leaves.
A broad column of steam rises from the central bed and spreads against the glass overhead, fanning out and thinning at the edges.
The inner surface of the door glass is fogged solid, only the brass push-plate showing through where warmth from a hand once cleared it.
Condensation on the angled glazing bars runs inward along their groove and drips from the lowest point in a steady tick.
The heated pipes themselves are barely visible through the haze at floor level, present only as a warm orange line in the white.
Every horizontal surface in the upper ironwork is wet, the flat tops of the purlins holding thin trembling films of collected steam.
Water gathering at the low point of a bowed pane has formed a lens of it there, distorting the view through that section of glass.
Moisture gathers on the underside of the brass crossbar and swells into a slow drip that ticks against the iron below.
The vent slot at the apex is ringed with condensation, a dark wet frame against the pale sky beyond.
Beads have formed along every chain link and catch the diffuse light as small bright points in the grey air.
A low cloud of steam pools in the corner where the two runs of glass meet, thicker there than anywhere else.
The brass rail along the upper walk has gone dark with wet and holds a solid film of water along its flat top.
Overhead, where two panes meet the central rib, the condensation runs together and drips in a fine steady curtain.
Warm breath rises off the open surface of the tank and spreads sideways under the glass above it.
The iron stay rods are filmed with moisture from end to end, their threads beaded and their nuts furred with damp.
Mist has settled into the lower beds and sits level with the lip of each trough, a white still layer.
The whole middle section of the house floats in a soft diffuse brightness where steam and light are barely separable.
A slow trickle finds the lowest point of the gutter and falls from there in a thin bright thread to the grating.
The haze thickens visibly above the heating pipes, rising in faint pulses as the pressure shifts inside them.
Glass squares on the roof have gone fully opaque with condensation, white and even, admitting only a general pale glow.
Rivulets cross the inner face of the flank glass in wandering paths, each finding a seam and pooling briefly before moving on.
The cast iron column at the near end is dark and slick, its fluted surface sheeted with a film too thin to drip.
Damp has darkened the timber staging across its whole surface, the grain swollen and the colour deep as wet soil.
Steam from the open pipe runs along the ceiling glass, spreading flat before it cools and falls back as fine rain.
The air near the floor carries a distinct warmth that rises against the skin, heavy and close and smelling of wet earth.
Every horizontal ledge of the frame holds a narrow standing puddle, level and still, mirroring the glass above in miniature.
Condensation on the tall end pane has run so long it has left pale mineral traces, faint vertical lines in the dried paths.
The brass coupling at the bend in the supply pipe is ringed with a collar of tiny drops that tremble when the flow shifts.
Soft clouds of vapour roll slowly through the gap between the staging trestles and thin as they reach the cooler centre aisle.
The inner surface of the ridge cap runs with water all along its length, a continuous thin sheet moving toward the end stop.
Drips from the highest rib have struck the broad surface of the tank so many times the water there is pocked and never quite still.
A dense belt of steam hangs between the upper catwalk and the eave line, swallowing the detail of both in white softness.
Breath-warm air presses against the outer glass and raises a bloom of mist on the cold pane from outside.
The brass rail along the upper walkway sweats in long beaded rows, each drop fat and trembling before it falls.
Along the ridge, slow condensation gathers at the bolt heads and hangs there in perfect round drops.
Mist pools in the curved hollow of every broad leaf and sits there still and white in the heavy air.
The vent at the end wall leaks a thin ribbon of cooler air that cuts a brief clear lane through the haze.
Rivulets branch and re-join on the slanted roof glass, finding new paths down with each new minute.
A fine grey sweat has broken out across all the lower ironwork, darkening it from bright to deep.
Steam rises off the open water butt in slow spirals that flatten and spread before they reach the ribs.
The chain hanging from the ceiling pulley is wet its full length and drips steadily from its lowest link.
Glass panels in the lower run are fogged from sill to midpoint, the upper halves still faintly clear.
Hot air pushes out through the cracked roof vent and vanishes into the cooler grey above.
Moisture has pooled in the angle between the floor channel and the stone sill and sits there without moving.
The smell of wet soil and warm iron fills the whole length of the house from end to end.
A slow drip from a rib joint has laid a dark stain across the wide flagstone beneath it.
Condensation on the curved end glass gathers at the lead strips and runs down them in thin bright threads.
The air near the boiler end shimmers faintly where the heat is greatest, bending the far glass in a soft wave.
Pale steam rolls over the rim of the open propagation tank and spreads across the path stones.
Every bolt and screw along the main spine carries its own bright bead of water by mid-morning.
The outer surface of the inner partition glass runs dry while its far face sheets with condensation.
Water has darkened the brick base wall along its top course, soaked up from the wet floor over many hours.
Vapour thickens visibly between the rows of raised beds, soft and white and shifting when the air stirs.
The lowest rib curves are running freely, water gathering speed as it reaches the bracket and dropping free.
A broad wet shadow spreads across the stone path where the overhang drips in an even line.
Dense mist lies against the far glass wall and flattens the depth of the house to a single pale plane.
Heat coming off the pipe along the back wall lifts the mist just above it into a slow rolling motion.
Brass fittings along the main pipe have gone green-dark at their joints where the wet has sat long enough to work on them.
The vent glass at the ridge stands cracked open and a thin tongue of steam curls through the gap and vanishes into the outside air.
Moisture has pooled in every low seam of the grating and sits there perfectly still, reflecting a narrow strip of the roof above.
The rail along the central path is slick and bright, its brass gone warm and slightly soft-looking under the coating of wet.
Overhead the ribs web the glass in dark lines and between them the condensation makes each pane its own small shifting mirror.
Where two pipes meet at the elbow below the bed, a slow persistent drip has stained the concrete dark in a long teardrop shape.
Heat from the pipes has set the air immediately around them shivering slightly, the ferns behind them bending and softening in the shimmer.
Along the lower pane at the far end a broad clear channel has been wiped by running water, the rest still dense with mist.
The smell of warm metal and wet soil thickens near the floor where the heat presses closest to the ground.
